Nicholas Nickleby. Serialized from 1838 to 1839, this novel follows a young gentleman named Nicholas after his father's death leaves him in poverty. Desperate for work, he is sent to Dotheboys Hall, a notorious Yorkshire boarding school where he is meant to teach. The school is run by Wackford Squeers, one of Dickens's most grotesque villains, a man whose beatings and systematic neglect of students embody institutional cruelty at its most brazen. Rather than submit to Squeers's abuse, Nicholas flees the school and embarks on a series of adventures across England. He joins a traveling theater company and experiences poverty and comic misadventure in equal measure. During his time at Dotheboys Hall, he befriends Smike, a poor boy who has been shamefully mistreated. Smike becomes Nicholas's loyal companion in his wanderings, though the boy's suffering carries a tragic weight that will haunt the novel. Among the more comic figures is Newman Noggs, a kind-hearted clerk, and Mrs. Nickleby, Nicholas's scatterbrained mother, whose naive chatter provides both humor and pathos. The novel is known for its loose, episodic structure. Rather than following a tightly plotted narrative, it's a series of interconnected misadventures that move between broad comic scenes, especially those involving the theater, and darker social satire focused on institutional cruelty. Through these episodes, Dickens demonstrates his developing critique of abuse of power and exploitation.
